title: Spring Lecture #9: Spring Boot Core
topics: Spring Core vs Spring Boot startup

questions.question: `@SpringBootApplication` is a combination annotation. Which three annotations does it roughly combine?
options: `@Component`, `@Autowired` and `@Bean`
`@RestController`, `@GetMapping` and `@Configuration`
`@SpringBootConfiguration`, `@EnableAutoConfiguration` and `@ComponentScan`
`@Configuration`, `@Lazy` and `@Scope`
questions.explanation: `@SpringBootConfiguration` marks the main configuration class (Boot's version of `@Configuration`), `@ComponentScan` finds your components from the main class's package downward, and `@EnableAutoConfiguration` applies Boot's ready-made configuration. Web annotations like `@RestController` are not part of it - Spring Boot is not only for web apps.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of using `spring-boot-starter-parent` as the `<parent>` of a Spring Boot project?
options: It provides compatible dependency and plugin versions plus build defaults, so you do not pick every version yourself
It starts the embedded Tomcat server when the project is built
It replaces Spring Core so that no IoC container is needed
It downloads Spring Initializr into the project
questions.explanation: The parent supplies managed versions of dependencies and plugins, the Java version setting, encoding and other build defaults, which reduces version-mismatch problems when you add libraries like Jackson or Hibernate. Starting a server is the job of a web starter plus auto-configuration at runtime, and Spring Boot always builds on Spring Core.

questions.question: You are converting the lecture's Spring Core `Main` (which called `context.getBean(OrderService.class).placeOrder()`) into a Spring Boot console app. What is the idiomatic way to call `placeOrder()` once the application has started?
options: Call `new OrderService(new PaymentService()).placeOrder()` inside `main`
Put the call in `OrderService`'s constructor so it runs when the bean is created
Annotate `placeOrder()` with `@SpringBootApplication`
Create a `@Component` that implements `CommandLineRunner`, inject `OrderService` through its constructor, and call it in `run()`
questions.explanation: `CommandLineRunner.run()` is called after the application context is created and ready, and the runner gets `OrderService` by normal dependency injection. Creating objects with `new` bypasses Spring, and doing work in a constructor runs it while the context is still being built.

questions.question: The classes below are in the packages shown in the comments. What happens when the application starts?
options: It starts normally, because all classes share the root `in.strikes`
Startup fails: `PaymentService` is outside `in.strikes.app` and its sub-packages, so it is not scanned and `OrderService` cannot get its dependency
It starts, but `OrderService` receives `null` for `paymentService`
It starts only if `PaymentService` is renamed to end with `Service` in its bean name
questions.explanation: The `@ComponentScan` inside `@SpringBootApplication` starts at the main class's package (`in.strikes.app`) and covers its sub-packages only, so `in.strikes.service` is skipped. Constructor injection then has no `PaymentService` bean and startup fails. Fix it by moving the main class to the root package `in.strikes` (best practice) or using `scanBasePackages = "in.strikes"`.

questions.question: Ignoring Spring Boot's log lines, what does this console application print? (`PaymentService.pay()` prints "Payment completed".)
options:
Starting
Payment completed
Order placed
Main finished

Starting
Main finished
Payment completed
Order placed

Payment completed
Order placed
Starting
Main finished

Starting
Main finished
questions.explanation: `SpringApplication.run()` builds the context and calls all `CommandLineRunner`s just before it returns, so the runner's output appears between "Starting" and "Main finished". The runner is a scanned `@Component`, so it definitely runs; nothing executes before `main` starts.

questions.question: What is the difference between `@ComponentScan` and `@EnableAutoConfiguration` in a Spring Boot application?
options: `@ComponentScan` applies Boot's default beans, while `@EnableAutoConfiguration` finds your `@Component` classes
They do the same thing; `@EnableAutoConfiguration` is just the newer name
`@ComponentScan` is only for web controllers, while `@EnableAutoConfiguration` is for services
`@ComponentScan` finds your own annotated classes; `@EnableAutoConfiguration` applies Boot's pre-written configuration when its conditions match
questions.explanation: Component scanning discovers your code (`@Component`, `@Service`, `@Repository`, `@Controller`...). Auto-configuration applies configuration classes shipped by Spring Boot or starters, based on the classpath, existing beans and properties. The first option swaps the two roles, and scanning is not limited to controllers.

questions.question: A new Spring Boot project has only `spring-boot-starter` as a dependency. It starts, runs its `CommandLineRunner`, and then exits; no "Tomcat started on port 8080" ever appears. A teammate thinks the project is broken. What is actually happening?
options: Tomcat crashed silently; the port is probably blocked by another program
No web classes are on the classpath, so auto-configuration treats it as a console app; adding the web starter would bring in web classes and an embedded server
Spring Boot only supports web applications, so the project is misconfigured
`@SpringBootApplication` must be given `web = true` to start a server
questions.explanation: Auto-configuration decides from the classpath: with no web server or Spring MVC classes, Boot does not configure a web server, and the app behaves like a normal console program that finishes when its work is done. Spring Boot is not only for web APIs. Adding the web starter changes the classpath, and Boot then starts an embedded server such as Tomcat.

questions.question: Assume `PaymentAutoConfiguration` is shipped by a starter and registered as an auto-configuration, and `PaymentGateway` is an interface on the classpath. What does the runner print?
options: DefaultPaymentGateway
Nothing - startup fails because two `PaymentGateway` beans exist
RazorpayGateway
DefaultPaymentGateway, because auto-configured beans always override user beans
questions.explanation: User-defined beans are registered before auto-configuration is evaluated. `@ConditionalOnClass` matches, but `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` sees that a `PaymentGateway` bean (`myGateway`) already exists, so the default is not created. Only one candidate remains, so there is no ambiguity - this is how Boot lets your configuration win.

questions.topic: Spring Core vs Spring Boot startup
questions.question: Migrating the lecture's `SpringCoreDemo` to Spring Boot, a teammate adds `@SpringBootApplication` to a main class in `in.strikes` and deletes the whole `AppConfig` class (which had `@ComponentScan("in.strikes")` and a `@Bean` method returning `new UserService()`; `UserService` has no annotations). Later, injecting `UserService` fails with "no qualifying bean". Why?
options: `@SpringBootApplication` does not perform component scanning, so `OrderService` and `PaymentService` were also lost
Spring Boot requires every bean to be declared in `application.properties`
Auto-configuration only creates `UserService` when a web starter is present

Scanning still finds the `@Component` classes, but `UserService` was only registered by the deleted `@Bean` method; auto-configuration never creates your own classes, so the `@Bean` method must be kept (e.g. in a `@Configuration` class or the main class)
questions.explanation: `@SpringBootApplication` replaces the manual `@ComponentScan`, so `OrderService` and `PaymentService` are still found. But a plain class registered via `@Bean` is not a component, and auto-configuration only applies Boot's own pre-written configurations. Keep the `@Bean` method in a `@Configuration` class, or in the main class, which works because it carries `@SpringBootConfiguration`.

questions.question: Which statement best describes how Spring Boot auto-configuration decides what to configure?
options: It applies every auto-configuration class it knows about, then removes beans that fail at startup
It applies pre-written configuration only when conditions match - e.g. a class is on the classpath, a bean is missing, or a property is enabled
It reads your source code and generates configuration classes for it at compile time
It replaces any bean you define with Boot's own default implementation
questions.explanation: Auto-configuration is "pre-written configuration + condition-based activation": checks like `@ConditionalOnClass` and `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` decide whether each configuration or bean applies. That is why adding a dependency changes behaviour without code changes, and why your own beans normally take precedence instead of being replaced.
